requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 937 | Request Title - Conversation View: Consistent message order | Request Description - Please correct me, but as far as I can tell, messages are sorted by time of arrival. However, since the messages are transported either via SMS or via Google Cloud Messaging, both of which don't guarantee ordering, messages may appear in the wrong order. This means that chat participants may see deviating orders of messages, replies to messages they don't even see. verdict.text:
On missing-slot detection, Track 1 is measurable here, but only for scope (34 gold-missing) and condition (21). Actor, modalVerb and action have support of 1, 1 and 4, so their recall of 1.0 or 0.5 reflects one to four cases and supports no conclusion. On the two measurable slots, CoT flagged a genuinely missing slot only about a third to two fifths of the time, which looks like heavy silent filling.

Much of that apparent fabrication is likely a format artifact rather than invented content. In 4333-Signal and 42-Mastodon the output contains no scope or condition text at all, yet both slots are scored "filled". The LLM simply omitted the placeholder that the humans always write, so the scorer seems to treat "no `<MISSING_SCOPE>` tag" as "filled". Real fabrication does occur, but it is rarer than the numbers suggest. 4031-Signal invents the condition "While media downloads are running", and 4230-Signal recasts the source's condition as a scope ("For each oversized text"). The scope flag rate of 0.32 is therefore probably an underestimate of the model, and it cannot be trusted until omission and filling are scored separately.

The more consistent behavioural failure runs the other way, and it is under-filling. The humans almost uniformly render the implied actor and modal as "the App must". CoT instead emits `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>` in roughly a third of implied cases (12 of 29 and 11 of 34), as in 4031, 4333, 5555 and 42-Mastodon. This drives all 12 "LLM incomplete, gold complete" verdict disagreements. It also suggests the chain-of-thought makes the model over-literal about what the text explicitly states. Condition shows a smaller version of the same thing: in 5555, 801, 175 and 4230 the model dropped conditions the humans extracted. The gold is itself unstable there, since one annotator marked 175's condition missing.

On similarity, the LLM sits below the human-human ceiling on every measure. It reaches about 81% of the ceiling on sequence ratio, 75% on Jaccard and 92% on cosine. With 35 requirements, the sequence-ratio gap of about 0.12 is roughly three standard errors, so it is probably real. However, the human ceiling is inflated by a shared boilerplate prefix that the LLM does not reproduce. The much smaller cosine gap suggests the semantic content is close to human quality and the shortfall is largely template conformance.

The Paska smells mostly measure the same placeholder problem. "Not requirement" (10 of 17 failures) appears almost wherever actor and modal placeholders replace a real subject and verb, because Paska cannot parse a system response from them. Pass rate is 0.74 for outputs the LLM considered complete against 0.25 for incomplete ones. The cases of 83, 592 and 1504-Signal are legitimate non-requirements where the smell is deserved. The three "Not precise verb" hits are the only substantive content smells. The single non-atomic flag on 6457-Signal is one case and worth a manual look, nothing more.

With 35 mostly Signal items from the pre-filtered atomic subset, this run is indicative at best and should not be generalised to unfiltered requirements.

The most useful next step is to fix measurement before comparing strategies. Have the model emit all five slots explicitly, ideally as structured per-slot output, and score omission separately from filling. Tell it that "the App must" is the default for implied actor and modal. Then rerun Paska with placeholders normalised. After that, compare against zsl and fsl.
